notes:
These notes on 1 Samuel 10 were collected from the allowed sites. A few gaps first:
- I didn't find any NET Bible notes, Bible Odyssey pages, Orthodox (oca.org) material, or denominational Pentecostal, Lutheran or Anglican sources on this chapter.
- I didn't find any prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on it.
- The older commentaries on biblehub and studylight don't say which tradition each writer belongs to. Where I give a tradition label, it comes from my own knowledge, not from the page, and I've marked it as such.
- My copy of Gill stopped after v. 11.
- Verses with nothing on them are left out.

---

**v. 1 (anointing, kiss, "His inheritance")**
- Guzik: What happened to Saul's head and body was a picture of what God did in him spiritually. The Holy Spirit was poured out on him, equipping him for the job of ruling as king over Israel. The kiss was not only a greeting; it was also a sign of Samuel's personal support of Saul. The anointing was private because it was not yet time to reveal Saul as king to the nation. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-10/
- Precept Austin: The only witnesses were Samuel and God. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-10-commentary
- Gill: Jewish sources say this was ordinary oil from a vial, not the tabernacle oil. They note that Saul and Jehu, anointed from a vial, had short reigns, while David and Solomon, anointed from a horn, had long ones. Gill adds that this may suggest Saul received a smaller measure of the Spirit. "His inheritance" shows Israel was still the Lord's, and Saul answered to Him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/10.htm
- Barnes: Samuel is answering the surprise Saul had already shown in 9:21. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/1_samuel/10.htm
- Matthew Henry: Saul was made a commander in war, which meant toil and danger. And since by him he ruled, and therefore must rule for him, in dependence on him, and with an eye to his glory. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Sa/1Sa_010.cfm
- Catholic: Augustine says all the kings anointed with "that mystical chrism," from Saul onward, were called the Lord's christs. Yet there was one true Christ, whose figure they bore. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/120117.htm Catholic Answers says Samuel anointed Saul with oil to show that he is a sacred person. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/1-2-samuel The Greek and Latin text on New Advent has a longer v. 1, with an added line about saving the people from their enemies (shown in the Knox English). https://www.newadvent.org/bible/1sa010.htm

**v. 2 (Rachel's tomb, Zelzah)**
- Guzik: the sign was specific enough to check, so Saul could be confident his anointing came from God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-10/
- Jamieson, Fausset & Brown: the detailed predictions were meant to confirm Saul's trust in Samuel as a prophet. They identify Zelzah as Bet-jalah. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/1Sa/1Sa_010.cfm
- Barnes calls Zelzah absolutely unknown. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/1_samuel/10.htm
- Gill: the tomb was on the road to Bethlehem, near the Judah–Benjamin border, so either tribe could be named. Kish was grieving most for Saul, possibly his only son. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/10.htm
- Matthew Henry: sending a man with a crown in view past a grave was a lesson in his own mortality. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/10-2.html
- Lange records Thenius's guess that the original read "at Zela," the burial place of Saul's father. https://studylight.org/commentaries/lcc/1-samuel-10.html

**vv. 3–4 (the three men, the bread)**
- Barnes: read "oak (or terebinth) of Tabor," not "plain." It may be the same as Deborah's oak below Bethel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/1_samuel/10.htm
- Gill: the goats, bread and wine were for sacrifice and drink offering at Bethel. Taking the bread was meant to teach Saul humility and kindness to the poor. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/10.htm Matthew Henry makes the same point: Saul must hereafter remember the time when he received alms. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Sa/1Sa_010.cfm
- Guzik: kings receive gifts, so this fittingly hinted at the kingship. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-10/

**v. 5 (Gibeah of God, the prophets, music)**
- Barnes: this is probably Saul's home town, Gibeah, called "of God" because of its high place. The note about the Philistine garrison may be the narrator's own aside. He also describes each instrument. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/1_samuel/10.htm
- Gill: he takes it as Geba, with a school of young prophets that Samuel encouraged. Here "prophesy" means singing praise, as the Targum renders it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/10.htm
- Guzik: their prophesying isn't necessarily saying that they were all predicting the future, but that they all spoke under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-10/

**v. 6 ("rush upon you," "a different person")**
- Barnes: the verb is used of fire spreading. Being "turned into another man" meant new mental power, a capacity for ruling (in the full text: one Saul lacked before). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/1_samuel/10.htm
- Guzik quotes Poole: the Spirit would "rush upon" Saul *for a season*, in contrast to the Spirit *resting* on someone (Num. 11:25; Isa. 11:2). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-10/

**v. 7 ("do as the occasion demands")**
- Gill: Saul was to use his new wisdom to prepare for the kingship. Some apply the phrase to royal dress or arms. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/10.htm
- A Precept Austin source sees here God's call for the use of our sanctified common-sense. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-10-commentary

**v. 8 (wait seven days at Gilgal)**
- Guzik: kings don't usually wait for anyone, so this showed the prophet's higher authority. Saul's later failure to wait would cause him trouble. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-10/
- Gill: this didn't happen right away. He links it to the Gilgal episode two years later (ch. 13), or reads it as a standing rule for any crisis. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/10.htm
- Matthew Henry: it showed Saul that he was upon his good behaviour. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Sa/1Sa_010.cfm

**v. 9 ("God changed Saul's heart") — the main point where interpreters differ**
- **A heart fitted for kingship, not conversion:**
  - Gill (Baptist; my label): not in a moral or spiritual sense, not a new heart, and a new spirit, as in conversion, but in a civil sense. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/10.htm
  - Hawker (Anglican; my label): these were "ordinary gifts of the Spirit"; Saul was not renewed in the spirit of his mind for all that. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pmc/1-samuel-10.html
  - Constable: it shouldn't be read as personal salvation, though some interpreters have taken this as Saul's conversion. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/10-9.html
  - The Biblical Illustrator: la inspiración es diferente a la regeneración ("inspiration is different from regeneration"). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/10-10.html
  - Whyte (Scottish Free Church; my label): the Spirit came on Saul for outward and earthly acts, but never for an inward change of heart. https://www.studylight.org/dictionaries/eng/wbc/s/saul.html
- **A real spiritual gift that was later lost:**
  - Benson (Methodist; my label): Saul felt a spirit of holiness, wisdom, and fortitude, to qualify him for the government of God's people; which afterward God took from him because of his sins. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/10-9.htm (named as Benson at https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/10-10.html)
  - Lange: in an important sense Saul was renewed, but this was damped and finally destroyed by the opposing force of his worldliness and self-seeking. https://studylight.org/commentaries/lcc/1-samuel-10.html
- **Charismatic / Calvary Chapel:**
  - Chuck Smith calls it a real kind of conversion kind of an experience. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/10-9.html
  - Guzik stresses that only God gave the new heart, not Samuel and not Saul himself. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-10/
- **Undecided:**
  - GotQuestions: was this salvation, or God simply overcoming Saul's reluctance? The Bible does not say. https://www.gotquestions.org/was-King-Saul-saved.html
  - Precept Austin compares it to the Spirit equipping Gideon and Jephthah. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-10-commentary

**v. 10**
- Ellicott: The changed heart was a fit home for that Divine Spirit. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/10-10.htm
- Gill: Saul joined their singing as if he had been trained. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/10.htm
- Matthew Henry warns: Saul among the prophets was Saul still. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/10-10.htm

**vv. 11–12 ("Is Saul also among the prophets?" / "Who is their father?")**
- Guzik: the proverb expressed surprise that someone had "got religion." "Who is their father?" means: who inspires the prophets? If God does, He can inspire Saul too. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-10/
- Gill: their real Teacher is the Lord. He compares this to Saul of Tarsus preaching (Acts 9:20). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/10.htm
- Barnes: a very obscure phrase. It could mean "what kind of leader admits Saul?" or, following other versions, "who is *his* father?" https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/1_samuel/10.htm
- Text note: JFB says the Septuagint reads, "Who is his father?" https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/1Sa/1Sa_010.cfm
- Lange: the reply rejects the idea that prophecy comes by birth. https://studylight.org/commentaries/lcc/1-samuel-10.html

**v. 13**
- Guzik: Saul prophesied without holding the office of prophet. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-10/
- Matthew Henry: he went to the high place to give thanks and to pray. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Sa/1Sa_010.cfm

**vv. 14–16 (Saul's silence with his uncle)**
- Barnes: Saul probably met his uncle at the high place. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/1_samuel/10.htm
- Matthew Henry: by keeping the secret Saul showed he had another heart, a heart fit for government. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Sa/1Sa_010.cfm
- Guzik: either wisdom (waiting for God to reveal him) or fear after a spiritual high. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-10/

**vv. 17–19 (Mizpah speech)**
- Guzik: God showed He was still well able to be their king. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-10/
- Precept Austin connects it to the first commandment. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-10-commentary
- Matthew Henry: some see Israel's stubbornness here as foreshadowing the rejection of Christ. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Sa/1Sa_010.cfm
- Barnes: "thousands" means families. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/1_samuel/10.htm

**vv. 20–21 (the lot)**
- Guzik: the lot didn't make Saul king. It simply confirmed the word of the LORD through Samuel. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-10/
- Barnes: the wording matches Joshua 7 (Achan). Matri isn't named anywhere else. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/1_samuel/10.htm

**vv. 22–23 (hidden among the baggage)**
- Guzik sees healthy humility. He cites Spurgeon's sermon "Hiding Among the Stuff," which applies it to people who hide from a heavenly crown. Saul's height made him "the king from central casting." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-10/
- Matthew Henry: Saul hid because he felt unfit, feared envy, and knew the request for a king was sinful. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Sa/1Sa_010.cfm
- Barnes: the baggage was the camp's wagon area. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/1_samuel/10.htm
- Catholic text: the Knox translation on New Advent has Saul hiding "in his tent." https://www.newadvent.org/bible/1sa010.htm

**v. 24**
- Precept Austin: Samuel stresses that Saul is the LORD's choice. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-10-commentary

**v. 25 (rights of kingship written down)**
- Barnes: a bill of rights (in the full text: one limiting the king's power), possibly a copy of Deuteronomy 17:14–20, kept by the ark. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/1_samuel/10.htm
- Guzik also suggests Deuteronomy 17. https://es.enduringword.com/comentario-biblico/1-de-samuel-10/
- Precept Austin: Samuel dismissing the people shows he still held authority. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-10-commentary

**v. 26**
- JFB: these men feared God and regarded allegiance to their king as a conscientious duty. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/1Sa/1Sa_010.cfm
- Hawker: "touched" means God made them inclined to respect Saul; no saving change of grace is meant. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pmc/1-samuel-10.html

**v. 27**
- Barnes: the "gift" (minchah) was a token of homage. Saul hid his resentment until the Nahash crisis. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/1_samuel/10.htm
- Guzik: Saul wisely didn't treat critics as enemies. https://es.enduringword.com/comentario-biblico/1-de-samuel-10/
- Precept Austin compares him to Christ, patient in suffering. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-10-commentary

---

**Modern critical view (whole chapter, from a Catholic source)**
- The Catholic Encyclopedia describes the critical theory that Samuel combines two accounts of Saul's rise. In one, Samuel resists a king and Saul is chosen by lot; in the other, Samuel anoints him willingly. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/08647b.htm
- Its Saul article calls the narrative composite. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/13486d.htm
